title: Childhood exposure to interparental conflict and adolescent mental health difficulties: The mediating role of self-regulation difficulties.
abstract: Interparental conflict (IPC) in early childhood is associated with mental health difficulties in adolescence. General psychological processes such as self-regulation that may underpin this relationship are important to understand during this developmental stage. The aim of the study was to investigate whether indicators of self-regulation difficulties in middle childhood, including (a) difficulties with persistence, (b) emotional reactivity, (c) behavioral disinhibition, and (d) sleeping difficulties, mediated the relationship between IPC in early childhood and mental health difficulties (anxiety and depressive symptoms; antisocial behavior) in adolescence. A second aim was to determine whether child sex moderated the associations between IPC, self-regulation difficulties, and mental health difficulties. Structural equation modeling using data from a population-based Australian sample (= 9,476) supported a mediation model where higher IPC at age 4-5 years was associated with higher indications of self-regulation difficulties at age 10-11 years, which in turn predicted higher depressive symptoms, anxious symptoms, and antisocial behavior at age 14-15 years. Evidence of moderation by child sex was found. The relationship between IPC, indicators of self-regulation difficulties, and antisocial behavior was stronger for males than females, while the relationship between indicators of self-regulation difficulties and internalizing outcomes was stronger for females compared to males. These results are interpreted using perspectives on biopsychosocial development, and implications for intervention at multiple time points are discussed.
